analysis.one_liner: Permanently cuts the corporate tax rate while giving families temporary tax cuts that mostly expire after 2025.
analysis.headline: It became Public Law 115-97 on December 22, 2017, after passing the House 227-205 and the Senate 51-49, with no Democrats voting for it in either chamber.
analysis.plain_summary: This law cuts the corporate tax rate from 35% to 21% permanently, and temporarily (through 2025) lowers most individual tax rates, doubles the child tax credit to $2,000, and nearly doubles the standard deduction. It creates a 20% deduction for owners of pass-through businesses, moves the U.S. to a largely territorial system for taxing corporate foreign earnings, and lets companies bring home overseas profits at reduced rates of 15.5% or 8%. It caps the state and local tax deduction at $10,000, repeals the penalty for going without health insurance, doubles the estate tax exemption to $10 million, and opens part of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to oil drilling.
analysis.who_benefits: Shareholders of large corporations get a permanent rate cut from 35% to 21%. Owners of partnerships, S corporations, and LLCs get a 20% deduction on business income through 2025. Wealthy households get a lower top rate (39.6% to 37%), a doubled estate tax exemption, a bigger alternative minimum tax exemption, and relief from the itemized-deduction limit. Working families get a doubled child tax credit and a larger standard deduction, but those provisions are temporary.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Corporations, business owners, and high earners

how_it_helps.text: Permanently lowers the corporate tax rate from a maximum of 35% to a flat 21% for tax years beginning after 2017.
Doubles the child tax credit to $2,000 per child under 17, with up to $1,400 refundable for lower-income families, and adds a $500 credit for other dependents through 2025.
Nearly doubles the standard deduction to $24,000 for married couples and $12,000 for single filers through 2025.
Allows owners of pass-through businesses (partnerships, S corporations, sole proprietorships) to deduct 20% of qualified business income through 2025.
Lowers the top individual rate from 39.6% to 37% through 2025 and doubles the estate and gift tax exemption from $5 million to $10 million per person.
Lets U.S. companies bring back accumulated overseas profits at reduced rates of 15.5% for cash and 8% for reinvested earnings, payable over eight years.

analysis.who_pays: Future taxpayers, because the individual cuts are written to expire after 2025 while the corporate cut is permanent, and the cost shows up as larger deficits. Filers in high-tax states lose part of the state and local tax deduction to the $10,000 cap. Taxpayers who go without health insurance no longer face a penalty, which the bill's authors counted as deficit savings and which the health insurance industry counted as lost customers. Millions of acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain are opened to oil and gas leasing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Future taxpayers, high-tax-state filers, uninsured households

drawbacks.text: The individual rate cuts, child tax credit increase, and estate tax doubling are temporary and expire after 2025, while the corporate rate cut to 21% has no expiration date.
Caps the deduction for state and local taxes at $10,000 per year, which raises taxes for filers who pay more than that, concentrated in high-tax states.
Suspends the deduction for personal exemptions (about $4,150 per person), which partially offsets the larger standard deduction, especially for large families.
Repeals the Affordable Care Act penalty for individuals who fail to maintain health coverage.
Switches inflation adjustments to the chained CPI, a slower-growing inflation measure, so tax brackets and credits rise more slowly over time than they otherwise would.
Suspends miscellaneous itemized deductions, including unreimbursed employee expenses such as tax preparation fees.
Requires the Interior Department to hold at least two oil and gas lease sales covering at least 400,000 acres each in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain within ten years.
Caps the medical expense deduction floor at 7.5% of income only for 2017 and 2018; it returns to 10% after that.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Most working families will see a smaller tax bill in the near term from the doubled child credit and larger standard deduction, but those benefits are written to vanish after 2025. The corporate rate cut is permanent, and the pass-through and estate-tax provisions overwhelmingly benefit higher-income business owners and heirs. The $10,000 state and local tax cap and the slow inflation adjustment push the other direction for some families over time. The overall design gives lasting relief to capital and temporary relief to wages, with the long-run cost carried by future taxpayers through larger deficits.

outcome.mechanism: It passed both chambers on near party-line votes through a fast-track budget process that needed only a simple majority in the Senate, and the President signed it on December 22, 2017.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced November 2, 2017, and reported amended by the House Ways and Means Committee on November 13.
The House Rules Committee structured debate so the bill was closed to amendments, allowing only a motion to recommit.
The House passed it 227-205: all 227 voting Republicans in favor, all 192 voting Democrats opposed, with 13 Republicans voting no.
In the Senate, Democrats offered at least ten motions to send the bill to the Finance Committee with instructions; every one was rejected, with Republicans voting unanimously against each.
The Senate passed its version 51-49; Senator Corker of Arkansas was the only Republican to vote no, and every Democrat and both independents voted no.

A conference committee of House and Senate negotiators filed the final compromise report on December 15, adding the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge oil leasing program and setting the corporate rate at 21% rather than 20%.

The Senate sustained budget points of order against part of the conference report, striking those provisions, then passed the remainder 51-48; the House then agreed to the Senate amendment 224-201, with 12 Republicans voting no.
The President signed the bill on December 22, 2017, and it became Public Law 115-97.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations and their shareholders, pass-through business owners, and high-income households came out ahead with permanent or long-lasting tax reductions, while the tax cuts written for ordinary families are the ones set to expire.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporations, business owners, and high earners

sides.party_line_note: Every roll-call vote on the bill split almost entirely by party: House passage was 227 Republicans and no Democrats in favor, Senate passage was 51-49 with Senator Corker the lone Republican no, and final votes saw zero Democratic support in either chamber.

industries.note: The bill permanently cuts the corporate rate from 35% to 21%, creates a largely territorial system for foreign earnings, and lets companies repatriate accumulated overseas profits at 15.5% or 8% rates. Shareholders capture the gain while the revenue loss adds to deficits that future taxpayers absorb.

industries.industry: Pass-through business owners (partnerships, S corps, LLCs, real estate)
industries.note: A new 20% deduction on qualified business income, available through 2025, primarily benefits owners rather than employees. The deduction is excluded for large service businesses like law and finance above income thresholds, but not for real estate.

The top rate falls from 39.6% to 37%, the estate tax exemption doubles to $10 million per person, the corporate AMT is repealed, and the limit on itemized deductions is suspended. Most of these provisions run through 2025.

The bill orders at least two lease sales of at least 400,000 acres each in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain and allows up to 2,000 surface acres of production facilities, while increasing Gulf offshore revenue sharing to Gulf states and scheduling a Strategic Petroleum Reserve sale.

Repealing the individual mandate penalty removes a financial incentive for people to buy coverage, costing insurers customers and narrowing the risk pool, while uninsured households save the penalty amount. The bill does not otherwise regulate insurers.
The bill lowers federal excise tax rates on beer, wine, and distilled spirits through 2019, a straightforward tax cut for brewers, wineries, and distillers of all sizes.
A 1.4% excise tax is imposed on the net investment income of certain private colleges with at least 500 tuition-paying students, directed at the largest endowments.
